subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Key studies: Bartlett (1932); Peterson and Peterson (1959)

questions.q: What are the three basic processes involved in memory?
questions.explain: Memory works through encoding (taking information in), storage (holding it) and retrieval (getting it back out).

questions.q: Which statement best describes encoding?
options: Converting information into a form that can be held in memory
Holding information over a period of time
Recovering stored information when it is needed
Losing information that was once stored
questions.explain: Encoding is the process of changing sensory input into a form (e.g. acoustic or semantic) that memory can store.

questions.q: A student recalls a phone number they were told earlier. Which memory process are they using?
questions.explain: Retrieval is bringing stored information back into conscious awareness when it is needed.

questions.q: What is the approximate capacity of short-term memory?
questions.explain: Miller found short-term memory holds roughly 5 to 9 (7 plus or minus 2) items.

questions.q: Approximately how long can information be held in short-term memory without rehearsal?
questions.explain: Without rehearsal, short-term memory holds information for only around 18 to 30 seconds before it is lost.

questions.q: How is information mainly coded in long-term memory?
options: It is not coded at all
questions.explain: Long-term memory codes information mainly by its meaning (semantically).

questions.q: Short-term memory is thought to code information mainly by:
questions.explain: Short-term memory tends to code information acoustically, which is why acoustically similar items are easily confused.

questions.q: What is anterograde amnesia?
options: An inability to form new long-term memories after an event or injury
Loss of memories from before an injury
A complete loss of all memory
A temporary loss of short-term memory only
questions.explain: Anterograde amnesia is the inability to store new long-term memories following brain damage.

questions.q: After a car accident, a man cannot remember events from the years before the crash. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories formed before the injury or event.

questions.q: Which of the following is a feature of long-term memory rather than short-term memory?
options: A potentially unlimited capacity and duration
A limited capacity of about 7 items
A duration of only a few seconds
questions.explain: Long-term memory is thought to have an unlimited capacity and can last up to a lifetime, unlike the limited short-term store.

questions.q: Who proposed the theory of reconstructive memory in 1932?
questions.explain: Bartlett (1932) proposed that memory is reconstructive rather than an exact copy of events.

questions.q: In Bartlett's theory, what is a schema?
options: A mental framework of prior knowledge that shapes how we remember
An exact recording of an experience
A part of the brain that stores memories
questions.explain: Schemas are packages of prior knowledge that influence how new information is understood and recalled.

questions.q: Participants in Bartlett's study changed the unfamiliar word 'canoe' to the more familiar 'boat' when recalling a story. Which effect of reconstructive memory does this show?
options: Distortion of detail to fit existing schemas
questions.explain: Recall becomes distorted as unfamiliar details are altered to fit the person's existing cultural schemas.

questions.q: Which story did Bartlett use to investigate reconstructive memory?
questions.explain: Bartlett used the Native American folk tale 'The War of the Ghosts', unfamiliar to his British participants.

questions.q: According to the Multi-store Model, in what order does information pass through the memory stores?
options: Sensory register, then short-term memory, then long-term memory
Long-term memory, then short-term memory, then sensory register
Short-term memory, then sensory register, then long-term memory
Sensory register, then long-term memory, then short-term memory
questions.explain: Atkinson and Shiffrin proposed information flows from the sensory register to short-term memory and then to long-term memory.

questions.q: Who proposed the Multi-store Model of memory in 1968?
questions.explain: The Multi-store Model was proposed by Atkinson and Shiffrin in 1968.

questions.q: In the Multi-store Model, what process transfers information from short-term memory into long-term memory?
questions.explain: Rehearsal maintains information in short-term memory and, if prolonged, transfers it into long-term memory.

questions.q: A student pays attention to a word on the board, then repeats it over and over until it sticks. According to the Multi-store Model, attention and rehearsal move the word from:
options: The sensory register to short-term memory, then to long-term memory
Long-term memory back to short-term memory
Short-term memory to the sensory register
Long-term memory to the sensory register
questions.explain: Attention passes information from the sensory register to short-term memory, and rehearsal then transfers it to long-term memory.

questions.q: What type of material did Peterson and Peterson (1959) ask participants to remember?
options: Consonant trigrams (nonsense syllables such as WRT)
questions.explain: Peterson and Peterson used consonant trigrams so participants could not attach meaning to them.

questions.q: Why were participants in Peterson and Peterson's study asked to count backwards in threes after seeing each trigram?
options: To prevent them from rehearsing the trigram
To help them remember the trigram for longer
questions.explain: Counting backwards stopped rehearsal so the researchers could measure the natural duration of short-term memory.

questions.q: In Peterson and Peterson's study, recall of trigrams fell sharply as the interval increased, with very little recalled after about 18 seconds. What does this suggest about short-term memory?
options: It has a very short duration when rehearsal is prevented
It is not affected by rehearsal
questions.explain: The rapid drop in recall shows that short-term memory lasts only around 18 seconds without rehearsal.
